items.stem: Why does Mrs. Pumphery think the dog’s recovery is “a triumph of surgery”?

items.stem: What kind of a person do you think the narrator, a veterinary surgeon, is ? Would you say he is tactful as well as full of common sense ?
items.answer: Doctor Herriot was a veterinary surgeon. He had a deep regard for Mrs. Pumphrey and concern for Tricki. He was worried for the health of Tricki. Herriot took great care of Tricki at the surgery. He felt happy on watching Pricki improve. He is a person with human quality of being tactful and full of commonsense. It is his tact which makes Mrs. Pumphrey agree to send Tricki to the surgery. He felt happy on watching Tricki improve. At the surgery it is the triumph of Mr. Herriot which is mainly earned through his commonsense.

items.stem: Do you think Tricki was happy to go home ? What do you think will happen now ?
items.answer: No, I think Tricki was not happy to go home. At home Tricki had no company, no friends to play with but in the hospital he knew the pleasures of sharing his food and things and he played with other animals. He even enjoyed catching rats. Naturally, he would not feel comfortable at Mrs. Pumphrey’s house with no friends and no games at all.

items.stem: Do you think this is a real-life episode, or mere fiction? Or is it a mixture of both ?
items.answer: The story seems to be quite real because rich people overfeed their children. As Mrs Pumphrey loved Tricki like her own child she overfed him. She was very emotional towards the cute puppy and could not bear the separation from her doting pet. There is nothing unusual in a wardrobe of dresses for the dog as rich people believe in showing the world that they are very rich to spoil even their pets. Talk About It

items.stem: This episode describes the silly behaviour of a rich woman who is foolishly indulgent, perhaps because she is lonely. Do you think such people are merely silly, or can their actions cause harm to others ?
items.answer: Mrs. Pumphrey was quite a rich lady. She had a small pet dog and named it Tricki. This episode describes the behaviour of the rich woman who indulges in foolish behaviour. It makes her keep such delicacies as cushions, toy, rubber rings, breakfast and all stuff. When Tricki is sent to the surgery, the delicacies are sent to the hospital. The tears in her eyes at Tricki’s departure are real. Every day she makes a phone call at the surgery. The worry and concern shown by her are merely silly. She is just busy in her own world and would not cause harm to others.

items.stem: Do you think there are parents like Mrs. Pumphrey?
items.answer: Of course, there are parents like Mrs. Pumphrey. They take too much care of their children. They never let their children play outside and overfeeds them when they seem weak. It results in making their children ill. They become hugely fat and often suffer from many diseases. Then they consult the doctors as Mrs. Pumphrey does. Children of such parents also suffer many mental diseases. They become coward. They lose confidence. In fact pampering is a crime for a child.

items.stem: What would you have done if you were (i) a member of the staff in Mrs Pumphrey’s household (ii) a neighbour ? What would your life have been like, in general ?
items.answer: (i) If I were a member of the staff in Mrs. Pumphrey’s household, I certainly would have tried to make her understand that pampering is bad. I would advise her not to show excessive love towards Tricki. (ii) If I were her neighbour I would again have advised her not to spoil the dog by pampering him. These actions of her certainly would cause harm to others also. In general, my life would have been simple as I certainly might have convinced Mrs. Pumphery that pampering is not good.

items.stem: What would you have done if you were in the narrator’s place ?
items.answer: If I were in the narrator’s place I would have done the same as the narrator had done to cure Tricki. Since Mrs. Pumphrey was very ignorant and was not realising the seriousness of matter, only this step was left to take Tricki out of the house. One must be very tactful and full of common sense while handling such a situation. The narrator knew that Tricki needed nothing else except plenty of exercises. Again the writer successfully came out of the temptation of keeping Tricki as a permanent guest. So, what the narrator had done was absolutely correct and I would have done the same.

items.stem: The story, A Triumph of Surgery is a powerful example of the importance of saying “no”. Explain.
items.answer: The story, ‘A Triumph of Surgery’ is a powerful example of the importance of saying “no”. When Dr. Herriot met Tricky with her owner Mrs. Pumphrey, he asked her to say “no” to overeating for Tricky as it would lead him to get ill. However, she was not able to say “no” to Tricky’s overfeeding and over-pampering and thus, had to send him to the hospital as he got seriously ill.

items.stem: What was the impact of the goodies that came for Tricki during his convalescence, on the household?
items.answer: The impact of all the goodies on the household was that they led to a period of indulgence and luxurious living. The household members, including the doctor and his partners, enjoyed the extra eggs, wine, and brandy. It added a sense of festivity to their daily routines, with lunch becoming a ceremonial occasion and evenings by the fire becoming more enjoyable.

items.stem: What was Mr. Herriot’s strict advice? Did Mrs. Pumphrey agree to his advice?
items.answer: Mr. Herriot’s strict advice to Mrs. Pumphrey was to restrain from giving her pet dog Tricky, unnecessary rich diet that would cause him serious illness and to give him plenty of exercises. No, Mrs. Pumphrey did not agree to his advice as she continued spoiling her dog’s health by giving him unrequited things like malt, cod liver, cupcakes, etc and no exercise.

items.stem: What do you think would happen to Tricki after he went back to Mrs Pumphrey?
items.answer: I think Tricki would again be over-pampered by Mrs Pumphrey. He might develop the same health issues gradually because Mrs Pumphrey was not aware of the actual treatment given to him.

items.stem: “I was really worried about Tricki this time.” Comment on the writer’s choice of beginning the story in this manner. What purpose does it serve?
items.answer: The writer chose this statement to begin the story to put the reader’s focus entirely on Tricki and his health from the very beginning of the lesson. Moreover, Tricki is the main character of the story.

items.stem: “Tricki’s only fault was greed”, says the narrator. What might be Mrs? Pumphrey’s “only fault”?
items.answer: Mrs Pumphrey’s only fault was her richness and over caring nature. She had provided luxurious things to an animal that replaced his actual needs and made him ill and obese.

items.stem: How did Mrs. Pumphrey and her servants behave when Tricki was being sent to the surgery?
items.answer: Mrs. Pumphrey began to cry loudly when Dr. Herriot carried Tricki in a blanket to his car. She gave out a despairing cry when the doctor moved off with Tricki. The entire staff was roused and maids-were rushed in and out bringing Tricki’s day bed, night bed, favourite cushions, toys and bowls. As Dr. Herriot drove away with Tricki, Mrs. Pumphrey, with a despairing cry, threw an armful of little coats through the window.

items.stem: Why did Mrs. Pumphrey call the doctor ? Or Why did Mrs. Pumphrey take Tricki to the doctor?
items.answer: Tricki was not eating anything for the past few days. He had refused even his favourite dishes and had bouts of vomiting. Moreover, he was spending his time lying on a rug, panting. He was not going for walks. All these symptoms, forced Mrs. Pumphrey to visit the doctor.

items.answer: Mrs. Pumphrey was a wealthy lady as she had many servants and maids. She also had a pet. She used to feed her pet with lot of dishes, sweets and snacks. Moreover, she had a separate room and wardrobe for her pet. All these things show that she was a rich lady.

items.stem: What was Mrs. Pumphrey’s reaction when Dr. Herriot suggested Tricki’s hospitalization?
items.answer: Dr. Herriot had made his plan in advance. So when Mrs. Pumphrey reported Tricki’s illness, he at once suggested him to be hospitalized for about a fortnight to be kept under observation. The poor lady almost swooned. She was sure he would pine and die if he did not see her every day.

items.stem: How did lunch become ‘a ceremonial occasion for Mr. Herriot and his partners’?
items.answer: Mrs. Pumphrey used to send extra eggs and wine and even brandy to build Tricki up. All these were consumed by Mr. Herriot and his partners. Thus for a fortnight, lunch became ‘a ceremonial occasion’ for them.

items.stem: What immediate step did Dr. Herriot take to save Tricki? Or “I think I know a cure for you.” What was Dr. Herriot’s ‘cure’ for Tricki?

items.stem: How do you know that Tricki had an affluent life?

items.stem: What were Mrs. Pumphrey’s queries when she called to enquire about Tricki in the hospital?
items.answer: Mrs. Pumphrey rang a dozen times for the latest bulletins on Tricki. Her queries were whether Tricki’s cushions were being turned regularly or was he wearing the correct coat according to the weather.

items.stem: “We are often over-indulgent towards people we care about.” Explain with reference to the context of the story “A Triumph of Surgery”.
items.answer: In the story “A Triumph of Surgery” from James Herriot’s collection, the over-indulgence towards those we care about is depicted through the relationship between Mrs. Pumphrey, a wealthy lady, and her Pekingese dog, Tricki. Mrs. Pumphrey’s deep affection for Tricki leads her to pamper him excessively with luxurious treats and little exercise, mistakenly believing that this is the best way to express her love. This indulgence results in Tricki becoming grossly overweight and lethargic, a direct consequence of his owner’s overbearing love and lack of understanding of his actual needs. The story illustrates how our affection can sometimes cloud our judgment, leading to actions that may not be in the best interest of those we care for. It’s a cautionary tale on the importance of balancing love with wisdom, especially when it comes to the health and well-being of others.

items.stem: Imagine that Mrs. Pumphrey from ‘A Triumph of Surgery’, reflects upon her behaviour, learns from her mistakes, and writes a diary entry about the consequences of overindulgence. Write this diary entry as Mrs. Pumphrey in about 120 words.
items.answer: January 20XX, Tuesday 9 p.m. Dear Diary, Today, I had a dreadful realisation. I love my dear Tricki, but I fear that that love has caused me to excessively indulge and pamper my dear pet. The sight of him, bloated and unhealthy, broke my heart. I believed that showering him with treats was a sign of care. But instead, I was causing him more harm than good. Thank goodness for Mr. Herriot. He aptly deduced that the reason for Tricki’s decline in health was my lack of strict boundaries with Tricki. When he noticed that I was not following his advice, he took Tricki away from me to take care of him. During Tricki’s absence, I began to reflect on my actions. Old habits die hard, but I will try my best to be a better caretaker for Tricki now that he is back home. Mrs. Pumphrey

items.stem: Imagine that one of Mr Herriot’s partners can understand dogs’ language and listen to Tricki on his last night with them (a) What might Tricki share about his experience? (b) How would he evaluate it in comparison to his home experience?
items.answer: (a) Tricki might share that he gets less to eat at the surgery but he feels more energetic there. He has to fight with other dogs to grab his share of the meal. Though his mates kick him and bowl him over, he loves and enjoys their company. He might say that he is getting to be quite stronger at the surgery. (b) He would evaluate from Tricki’s experience that overprotectiveness and overeating without exercise can make anyone unhealthy. We must understand that life is not about eating all the time. Besides every discomfort does not need medicine or surgery. Lifestyle disorders can be treated with the right routine and eating habits. He might conclude from Tricki’s experience that richness does not guarantee health and happiness.

items.stem: Give a brief character sketch of Mrs. Pumphrey. What values are reflected through her character ?
items.answer: Mrs. Pumphrey was a rich lady with a lot of love for pet dog, Tricki. She loved to live comfortably in a luxurious way. She took an extra care of Tricki by overfeeding him. She was not very intelligent as she was not able to make out that the excess of weight and the fur coats do not allow the dog to move and play. She thought that her loving pet was serious. She was so fond of her dog that she had got a wardrobe separate for daytime and night-time beds, and a number of lovely fur coats. She pampered Tricki by giving him the food, that should not be given to a dog. She was really a loving lady as the news about the surgery of her pet dog shocked her and her eyes brimmed with tears. She could not refuse delicious and favourite food to Tricki which made him overweight and inactive. Even in the hospital, she sent him eggs and brandy. Her fondness for the dog and extra care showed that she had motherly attitude towards Tricki.

items.stem: How did the ‘parting scene’ between Tricki and Mrs. Pumphrey’s household come to end ?
items.answer: Tricki, the dog was very ill. He had to be sent to the surgery for a fortnight. There was quite a sensation at the time of parting. Mrs. Pumphrey the owner, started wailing. The entire staff was roused. The maids rushed in and out. They ran to collect Tricki’s things. Mr. Herriot saw that his car could not hold all these things. So he sat in with Tricki and started his car. Mrs. Pumphrey was carrying a number of coats on her arm which she threw in through the window of Mr. Herriot’s car. Mr. Herriot reached the corner of the street. He looked in the mirror and noticed everybody was in tears.

items.stem: Herriot seems to be a duty-bound doctor who values others’ emotions’ than his personal interests. Elucidate the above statement. Mention those values of Herriot which you would like to emulate in yourself also and give reasons for the same.
items.answer: Herriot was a duty bound veterinary doctor. He used to visit Mrs. Pumphrey’s house regularly for the regular check-up of her dog Tricki. Mrs. Pumphrey was a very rich lady who had pampered her dog. Dr. Herriot was quite worried about Tricki’s health. He knew that the dog was over-fed by his owner. He advised Mrs. Pumphery to keep him off rich diet and give him a lot of exercise. But she didn’t bother. Hence, in order to improve Tricki’s health, he decided to take him away from Mrs. Pumphrey. He told her that Tricki needed a surgery. He made Tricki cut down his diet and made him do certain exercise which improved his health. Although he knew Mrs. Pumphrey was very rich and much attached to the dog, he did not take any advantage of it. He just performed his duties. We should also learn the same values in our life.

items.stem: Compare and contrast Tricki’s condition in the beginning and in the end of the story.
items.answer: In the beginning of his the story, we find Tricki to be extremely fat. His eyes were bloodshot and rheumy, while his tongue lolled from his jaws. He was lethargic and listless and never seemed to have any energy. So, tt was very difficult for him to move along the road. On the other hand, he was very greedy. He would not refuse food at any hour of the day. Therefore, as the days passed, his condition worsened. He even refused to touch food and did not want to go for walks. Because of his declining health, Tricki refused his favourite dishes and besides, he had bouts of vomiting. He spent all his time lying on a rug, panting. He didn’t want to do anything. He was in such a pathetic state that he could hardly wag his tail. Later, at the surgery when he was put down, he lay motionless on the carpet. He looked at the household dogs with dull eyes. The other dogs, after sniffing round him for a few seconds, found him to be an uninteresting object and ignored him. At this place, he was given no food but plenty of water on the first day. This place seemed to have had a positive impact on Tricki. Because within some days, Tricki ran about with the dogs, joining in the friendly scrimmages. Eventually, in two weeks, he had been transformed into a lithe, hard-muscled animal.

I think Mrs. Pumphrey’s extra-caring nature resulted in Tricki’s declined health. Such an attitude can be fatal for the health of their kins. One should not over care of them. Exercise and proper meal are important for one’s health. The same was taken care by Dr Herriot, which resulted in the speedy recovery of Tricki.

items.answer: Today has been a roller coaster of emotions for me. Meeting Mr. Anil changed my life. He didn’t see me as just another street kid; he saw potential in me and taught me the importance of trust, kindness, and honesty. He gave me a chance to learn to read and write, opening up a whole new world for me. But tonight, I made a huge mistake. I stole money from Mr. Anil, thinking only of the immediate gain. I’ve decided to go back to Mr. Anil tomorrow, return the money, and apologize. I’m scared, but I hope he can forgive me and give me another chance. items.stem: Examine how Anil’s identity as a writer could have contributed to his understanding of Hari Singh.
items.answer: Anil’s identity as a writer plays a significant role in the narrative and contributes to his understanding of Hari Singh in several ways. Firstly, being a writer allows Anil to possess a heightened sense of observation and empathy. Writers often possess a keen understanding of human behaviour, enabling them to read between the lines and determine shades in people’s actions and expressions. This skill becomes crucial in Anil’s interaction with Hari Singh, as he could perceive more than what meets the eye. Additionally, Anil’s profession as a writer might have made him more open-minded and receptive to diverse experiences and personalities. Writers often explore a wide range of characters in their work, fostering a broader understanding of human nature. This openness could have enabled Anil to approach Hari Singh with empathy and without immediate judgment. Lastly, Anil’s familiarity with constructing narratives may have enabled him to appreciate the complexity of Hari Singh’s life story, recognizing the underlying factors influencing his actions.

items.stem: A character arc is the transformation or development of a character throughout a story and refers to the changes a character undergoes as a result of their experiences, challenges, and interactions with other characters. In the light of the above information, trace the character arc of the thief in Ruskin Bond’s ‘The Thief’s Story’, in about 120 words.
items.answer: The thief’s character arc in the story shows a transformation from a career criminal to a person who learns to trust and work hard for a living. At the beginning of the story, Hari Singh is portrayed as an experienced criminal who is focused on staying ahead of the law. He is initially attracted to Anil because he believes he can exploit the young man’s trusting nature. As the story progresses, he begins to develop a friendship with Anil, who teaches him how to cook, write, and read. This transformation of the thief’s character reaches a climax when he is presented with an opportunity to steal money from Anil but instead chooses to resist the temptation and considers the consequences of his actions. This is a significant change from the beginning of the story, when the thief was only interested in self-gain.

items.answer: Just like Ausable showed great ‘presence of mind’ or the ability to think quickly and act calmly and wisely in a situation of danger and surprise, we all must stick to our senses and wits and behave in a composed yet clever manner in times of crisis. I too remember having behaved in such a way some months back. While playing in the park one day, one of my friends fell from the swing and was hit hard on his head. He fainted and his head started bleeding. We were five friends playing in the park and there was nobody around us. Everybody was scared and started crying. I sent one of them to that boy’s place to call his parents and rushed to fetch my bag which had a water bottle in it. I sprinkled some water on my friend’s face after which he regained consciousness. By this time, his parents came and they thanked me for acting wisely in such a situation and took him to the doctor timely. My parents were also very impressed with me.

items.stem: Discuss what you would do in the situations described below. Remember that presence of mind comes out of a state of mental preparedness. If you have thought about possible problems or dangers, and about how to act in such situations, you have a better chance of dealing with such situations if they do arise. (i) a small fire starts in your kitchen. (ii) a child starts to choke on a piece of food. (iii) an electrical appliance starts to hiss and gives out sparks. (iv) a bicycle knocks down a pedestrian. (v) it rains continuously for more than twenty four hours. (vi) a member of your family does not return home at the usual or expected time.
items.answer: (i) Fire in a kitchen can make us turn panicky. Infact in kitchen there is a gas cylinder, which can burst any moment. If a small fire starts in our kitchen, the first step should be to close the regulator and try to open the doors and window of the kitchen. In such a situation we should also put off the main switch. If possible try to put sand over the fire. (ii) Food choked in the mouth of a child can be quite risky. Calm and patience are must for any kind of calamity. The child should be asked to keep quiet and his back should be rubbed softly. If need arises a glass of water can be given to drink. The child should be advised that while eating he should not talk. (iii) Electrical fires can be very dangerous. They can not be put off by throwing water. There can cause short circuit and even bring the whole structure down. In case of such fires, the foremost priority should be to put off the main switch. One should never touch any switch with wet hands and always keep your foot covered. (iv) If you are a passer-by and witness a pedestrian being knocked down. In such a situation, some people simply laugh and create fun. But you must act sensibly. Go near the pedestrian. Try to see where he has been hurt. If need arises, take him to the nearby doctor. At least try to give him first-aid. Such a good act will always pay you in later life. If the injury is serious, take him to the hospital and inform his relatives. (v) Continuous rain can also have some unforeseen consequences. The pipes can get choked and cause a kind of danger to the building structure. Call a plumber to get all the pipes checked. The road may form pits and become breeding grounds for mosquitoes. The danger of accident also increases. Try to form a group with friends of your own age. Sort of community participation would be of great help. Insecticides can be sprayed in stagnant water and water should be cleared off the roads. (vi) It is human nature to show worry for our near and dear ones. If a member of our family does not return home at the usual time then first of all we should check at the place where he was expected to go. After knowing about his time of departure, check with his friends and other associates. If no whereabouts are found out report at the nearest Police Station. You may suggest other such situations.

items.stem: Ausable was always one step ahead of everyone. Highlight any two instances from “The Midnight Visitor” when this holds true.

items.stem: Henry unintentionally saved Ausable’s life. Briefly comment.

items.stem: Ausable displays an acute sense of awareness of his surroundings. Justify with any two instances from the text.
items.answer: Ausable displayed an acute sense of awareness of his surroundings at two incidence. He was fully aware of his hotel room’s entrance and exit. He confirmed it already that his room did not have an attached balcony. He had calculated well in advance the time for the waiter’s arrival for room service.

items.stem: Why was Ausable confident that Max would never return ?
items.answer: Believing Ausable’s story about the balcony to be true, Max stepped out of the window. Ausable, however, had concocted a very convincing story, and knew that what awaited him was a drop from the sixth floor. Hence, he was confident that Max would never return.

items.stem: How and why did Max come inside Ausable’s room ?
items.answer: Max had come into the room using a pass key. He had come to get the secret report about some new missiles which, he was sure, was with Ausable.

items.stem: How did Ausable kill Max without using a weapon?
items.answer: Ausable was an intelligent spy. When he found Max waiting for him in his room, he made a story of a balcony under his window. He convinced Max about the balcony. And thus, when someone knocked at the door, Max fearing it to be the police, jumped out of the window and died.

items.stem: Why was Ausable angry with the hotel’s management?
items.answer: Ausable pretended to be angry with the hotel’s management to misguide Max. He said that he had complained to the hotel management to block off the balcony extended under the window of his room. They did not act upon and this was the second time in a month an intruder entered his room.

items.stem: Why did Fowler want to meet Ausable? Why was he disillusioned?
items.answer: Fowler was a very young and romantic writer. He wanted to meet Ausable, the secret agent to learn how Ausable tackled with some exciting events. He was disillusioned because he thought Ausable was an unfit secret agent on account of his fat body and American accent.

items.answer: Ausable made up a story very beautifully. He showed disappointment that in spite of his complaint to block off the balcony attached to his room, no action had been taken. He said that it was the second chance in a month that an intruder had entered his room through balcony.

items.stem: What role did the non-existent balcony play in the story “The Midnight Visitor’?
items.answer: The non-existent balcony plays a very important role in the story. It is on this balcony that Max jumps to save himself from being caught by the police but instead ends up being a dead man.

items.stem: How was Max outwitted by Ausable in the end of the story ‘The Midnight Visitor’ ?
items.answer: Ausable made Max believe that there was a balcony outside the window of his hotel room, when there was none. Ausable also made Max believe that the policemen were knocking at the door. Therefore, Max dropped out to the balcony to avoid the police but died due to the fall, six storeys below.

items.stem: “Despite his unusual appearance, Ausable’s presence of mind helped him get rid of Max.” Comment with reference to the story ‘The Midnight Visitor’.
items.answer: In “The Midnight Visitor,” Ausable, despite not fitting the stereotypical image of a cunning and physically agile secret agent due to his unusual appearance, showcases his exceptional presence of mind and quick thinking. When confronted by Max, an adversary, in his hotel room, Ausable cleverly invents a story about a non-existent balcony and an imaginary police arrival. His ingenious bluff about the hotel room being under surveillance with the police due to arrive through a fictional balcony convinces Max. This mental agility and the ability to think on his feet enable Ausable to outwit Max, leading to Max’s panicked attempt to escape through the supposed balcony, which results in his downfall. Ausable’s sharp mind, therefore, compensates for his physical appearance, proving that intellect and psychological tactics can be far more effective in espionage than mere physical prowess.

He had wished to meet Ausable because Fowler was a young and romantic writer who imagined a secret agent to be associated with mysterious figures in the night, the crack of pistols and drugs in the wine. Though Ausable’s appearance did not match that of a secret agent and he did not really fit the description of one, he was indeed a very intelligent and smart agent. Ausable understood Fowler’s disillusionment and told him to take cheer because he would presently see an important paper for which several people had risked their lives and that could well affect the course of history.

items.stem: How did Ausable use ‘the knock’ at the door in his favour? What light does this throw on his character?
items.answer: There was a sudden knock at the door. Ausable knew it that the water had come to serve the drink ordered by him. He used his presence of mind and informed Max that it would be the police. Even in the most difficult situation when a man was standing aiming a pistol at him, he did not lose his nerves. He said that he demanded extra police protection and asked them to check on him regularly so nothing went wrong with him. He said that the room was unlocked and the police would not hesitate to shoot Max. Max unwittingly jumped outside the room and .got injured. Thus Ausable with his sheer intelligence got through an unimaginable difficult situation.

items.stem: How did Ausable get rid of Max? Or How did Ausable fool Max and get rid of him?
items.answer: Ausable got rid of Max by using his intelligence, alertness and presence of mind. Max met his end by jumping out of a window, which Ausable said had a balcony outside, but there was no balcony and Max dropped down dead. Max’s own foolishness makes him an easy prey to Ausable’s clever thinking. When there was a knock on the door, Ausable told Max it was the police who had come to check on him. Max was convinced and in a bid to escape jumped out of the window without thinking.

items.stem: Give a brief character sketch of Fowler ? What are the values reflected in his character ?
items.answer: Fowler is a young romantic writer, who loves reading mysterious stories. He has a fantasy to meet a secret agent or to see mysterious figures in the night, the crack of guns, drugs in wine, etc. He is not much interested in meeting dull people. He gets easily bored and disappointed. Though he is a writer, he is very timid by heart. He easily loses his cool and gets nervous. The moment he enters Ausable’s room and his eyes meet Max with an automatic pistol in his hand, he is thrilled. He is scared, the moment he realises that it is a waiter and not the police who has knocked at the door. He wants to know about the man in the balcony. He has a horrible experience with Ausable tackling risky situations so calmly.

items.answer: Max was in Ausable’s room with a pistol in his hand. When there was a knock at the door Ausable convinced Max that it was police. He excited him to hide himself on the non-existent balcony. Max, in terror, jumped from the sixth floor and met his end. No, it cannot be called nonviolence. Ausable saved himself but led Max to death. He made him jump from the eight floor. He concocted the story of a non-existent balcony and convinced him to hide there. He trusted him and jumped to death. Violence should never be supported but in prevention of crime it is inevitable. We cannot tackle the criminals without the use of weapons and violence is inevitable.

items.answer: Wednesday May, 20xx 10:50 p.m. Dear Diary, Being a young and romantic writer, I have read many books depicting the heroic deeds of secret agents. I have always imagined them to be romantic, mysterious, smart and dashing people. So, I was thrilled when I got a telephonic appointment with Ausable, a very famous secret agent. He told me to meet him at a French music hall in the evening. I was happy because I was going to meet a renowned mysterious figure. But later, I was disappointed to see an extremely fat man wearing casual clothes. This secret agent spoke French and German passably with a slight American accent. In fact, the more time I spent in his company, the more I got bored and disillusioned. He lived in an ordinary hotel and used an ordinary telephone for the purpose of communication, nothing like the life I had imagined for a secret agent. I am disillusioned. Waiting for some action. In disappointment. Fowler

items.stem: Did you begin to suspect, before the end of the story, that the lady was not the person Horace Danby took her to be ? If so, at what point did you realise this and how ?
items.answer: Yes, I started to suspect, before the end of the story, that the lady was not the person Horace Danby took her to be. I realised this when the lady told Horace that she had forgotten the numbers to open the safe and she asked him to break open the safe. She also promised him that she would let him go if only he opened the safe. In fact on one would do this kind of act if she is the real owner of the house.

items.stem: What are the subtle ways in which the lady manages to deceive Horace Danby into thinking she is the lady of the house ? Why doesn’t Horace suspect that something is wrong ?
items.answer: The lady in the red dress was very clever. She was also a thief like Horace. She was also a good planner. She called the dog by its name. She told Horace that she had heard him from the top of the house. She also suggested him to go to some good doctor for the treatment of his hay fever. She threatened to call the police. There was a firmness in her voice. She showed full confidence. Thus Horace was trapped. Since he was a thief, he could not resist and he also did not get time to think. He was caught red haded and was so trapped in that he could not suspect that something was wrong.

items.stem: ‘Horace Danby was good and respectable-but not completely honest’, why do you think this description is apt for Horace ? Why can’t he be categorized as a typical thief ?
items.answer: Horace Danby was unmarried. He was about fifty years old. He was a good-natured man. Therefore, everyone liked him. He was fairly successful in his profession of lock making. As he lived peaceful so he was considered a respectable citizen. But he was not completely honest. He had a keen fondness of rare and expensive books. He needed a great deal of money to buy books. He can’t be described as a typical thief because he committed just one theft every year. Moreover, he would rob only rich people. He never hurt anyone and did not carry any weapons. He was submissive and did not want to go to the prison. So we can justify to say that he was not a typical thief.

items.stem: Horace Danby was a meticulous planner but still he faltered. Where did he go wrong and why ?
items.answer: Horace Danby robbed a safe every year which was enough to last for twelve months. He planned his robbery very meticulously. For two weeks he had been studying the complex situation of the house at Shotover Grange. In the magazine he had read the situation of rooms, electric wires, paths and its garden. He had studied the detailed plan of the drawing room. He had seen the housekeeper hang the key. He had even learnt the name of the dog. The only major mistake had been that he had not even once met the owner of the house. He did not know that the land lady was quite an old lady of sixty. If he had known the lady of the house than the lady in red could not have tricked him. The other mistake was that he had not cut the telephone wires. He also opened the safe without gloves, which left his fingerprint all over. He was easily found and arrested for the jewels robbery. Talk About It

items.stem: Do you think Horace Danby was unfairly punished, or that he deserved what he got ?
items.answer: Horace Danby was a thief but not a typical thief. He had planned robbery at Shotover Grange but not with any bad intention. In this story Horace was punished for the crime which he had not directly done. He had not got the jewels from the Grange Safe. It was his carelessness which had got him caught. He was held culprit and was arrested though he did not get a single jewel. The lady in red posed to be the mistress of the house. She made Horace open the safe. She took all the jewellery in her possession. So it is wrong to say Horace Danby was punished for his crime. He was unfairly punished.

items.stem: Do intentions justify actions ? Would you, like Horace Danby, do something wrong if you thought your ends justified the means ? Do you think that there are situations in which it is excusable to act less than honestly ?
items.answer: Intentions and actions go hand in hand. Intentions and actions are two sides of a coin. If we have good intentions then we will never stoop to do bad even if we are going to be rewarded high. No, I would not do anything wrong like Horace Danby. Even if I am being promised a rich reward, I would not do wrong acts. We know that even a bad company or witnessing a crime can be bad. Honesty is the best policy but still at times we have to keep aside true honesty. Suppose we have not completed our destined task then we have to make some untoward excuses. Such excuses can save us for the moment and save our prestige.

items.stem: “Horace Danby is a thief who was cheated by another thief.” Justify.
items.answer: Horace Danby’s portrayal in “A Question of Trust” reflects the irony of his situation. While he is indeed a thief, his trust is betrayed by another thief, Mr. Cornelius. This deception underscores the complexity of trust and the unpredictable nature of human behavior, even among criminals.

items.stem: How did the lady in red manage to outsmart and out maneuver the other thief, Horace Danby, by robbing the safe without leaving a single fingerprint ?
items.answer: The young lady in red was also a thief but she presented herself as the lady of the house. ... Horace thought that he was opening the safe for the lady of the house. He handed the jewels over to her and went out happily. He had forgotten to wear his gloves and left his fingerprints on the safe.

items.stem: What was Horace Danby’s hobby? How did he manage to fulfil it?
items.answer: Horace Danby had the hobby of collecting rare and expensive books. He managed to fulfill it by robbing a safe every year. Each year he planned carefully just what he would do to steal enough to last for twelve months, and secretly bought the books he loved through an agent.

items.stem: Why did Horace mistake the young lady for the mistress of the house ?
items.answer: The young lady snubbed the house-dog with authority as well as love. She stared at Horace with an imposing air of confidence. She spoke that she had returned just in time. Her manner of speaking and actions made Horace mistake her for the mistress of the house.

items.stem: What made Horace sneeze frequently at the house in Shotover Grange ?
items.answer: Horace had hay fever or was allergic to flowers. There was a great bowl of flowers lying on the table in the house he was supposed to rob in Shotover Grange. Therefore, he felt his nose tickle and he sneezed. He sneezed loudly whenever the smell of flowers came to him again and again in that house.

items.stem: What made Horace believe that the lady was the actual lady of the house ?
items.answer: The young lady had a quiet, firm voice. Entering the room, she walked gracefully to the fireplace and straightened the ornaments there as if she was the owner of the house. Her natural reaction and at ease behaviour, made Horace believe that she was the actual lady of the house.

items.stem: “Society must be protected from men like you.” Do you find this statement ironic ?
items.answer: The lady in the red dress was very shrewd and cunning. She talked about protecting the society from the criminals like Horace when in fact, the lady was the greater culprit. She had come into that house with the same intention as Horace, but had somehow made Horace the culprit when she was the one who had actually stolen the jewels from the house.

items.stem: What do you think is the meaning of the phrase ‘honour among thieves’ ?
items.answer: The phrase ‘honour among thieves’ means that amongst the thieves there ought to be mutual trust, and that thieves do not compromise the theft or activities of other thieves. They are supposed to be honest among fellow criminals and thus, honour each other’s feeling of trust.

items.stem: A small dog was lying in the kitchen. It stirred, made a noise, and moved its tail in a friendly way. (a) What is the name of the dog and where is the kitchen located ? (b) What tact did Horace apply here ?

items.stem: What did Horace Danby wonder about for a moment? What did he think and decide ?

items.stem: How often did Horace Danby commit a robbery every year? What did he do with the stolen material?
items.answer: Horace Danby robbed only one safe every year. Each year he planned carefully just what he would do. He stole enough to last him for twelve months and with the rest of the money be bought rare and expensive books, that he loved, through an agent.

items.stem: Why did Horace Danby feel sure of his success in that year’s robbery?
items.answer: Horace Danby felt sure of his success in that year’s robbery as he had been studying rooms, electric wiring, paths and gardens of the house at Shotover Grange for two weeks. He knew that the family was in London and the two servants who lived in the house had gone to watch movie that afternoon.

items.stem: What story did the lady tell Horace to get the jewels?
items.answer: The lady made up a story that before going to London, she promised her husband to take her jewels to their bank; but she left them there in the safe. She wished to put on the jewels to a party that night. Above all she had forgotten the numbers to open the safe. Thus she convinced Horace to open the safe.

items.stem: Why did the police arrest Horace Danby when he had not kept the jewels stolen from Grange safe?
items.answer: The police arrested Horace Danby even when he had not kept the jewels stolen from the Grange Safe because his fingerprints were all over the room. No one believed him when he said that the wife of the owner of the house had asked him to open the safe for her and his story was termed as utter ‘nonsense’.

items.stem: Why would Horace get angry when anyone talked on honour among thieves ?

items.stem: Why did Horace feel sure that year’s robbery at Shotover Grange would be as successful as all the others ?
items.answer: Horace Danby chose the house at Shotover Grange to commit his next burglary. He studied the design of the house carefully. He took note of the rooms, electric wiring, paths and garden. He also knew that the family had gone to London. He had seen the servants hanging the keys to the kitchen door and going to pictures.

items.stem: Why did the lady report to the police though she promised that she would not report to the police?
items.answer: The lady was very clever and shrewd. She promised Horace that she would not report to the police if he helped her in getting the jewels from the safe. Horace broke the safe and helped her. But she didn’t keep her promise as she was also a thief and did not want to get into trouble.

items.stem: Who do you think is the real culprit in the story ‘A Question of Trust’?
items.answer: Obviously the young lady who pretended to be the member of the family was real culprit. She innocently asked Horace to open the safe as she would need the jewels to wear in the party that day. Horace found himself trapped in a tricky situation and could not make out how to escape. He readily opened the safe; unwittingly leaving his fingerprints. He was arrested and nobody believed that the lady of house asked him to open the safe. It seems the young lady outwitted experienced Horace. She cheated and deceived Horace scrupulously.

items.stem: Horace stated that he robbed only those who had a lot of money. Was he really a threat to the society ? Did he lack the qualities of a good citizen ? Discuss the values he needs to imbibe to lead a path of righteousness.
items.answer: I don’t think Horace was a threat to the society. He never threatened anyone and rather stole for a very good reason. He used to rob a safe every year to pursue his hobby of getting rare and expensive books to read. He was not a professional thief. Moreover, he never harmed anyone. He was considered a good and honest citizen by everyone. He was about fifty years old and unmarried. He had all the qualities of a good citizen. He was not a criminal or a typical thief. He did so only to fulfil his need. He was an honest and good man. He believed in the lady’s story and gave away all the jewels to her. If he had been a criminal, he would have killed the lady or would have never handed the jewels to her.

items.stem: Horace Danby requested the lady to forget what she saw. Was Horace afraid of being caught ? Did he lack courage to accept his crime publicly? Explain the values one must imbibe to accept one’s mistake.
items.answer: Yes, Horace Danby was afraid of being caught. He lacked the courage to accept his crime publicly. He was not a professional criminal or thief. He was considered a good and honest man by everyone. He was about fifty years old and unmarried. His house was looked after by a housekeeper. He used to rob only one safe every year to pursue his habit of getting rare and expensive books to read. He used to rob only those who were rich. He had a good reputation in the society and hence did not want anyone to know about his crimes. Although he helped the lady, but was caught by the police for the crime he did not commit. He learnt from his mistake.

items.stem: Describe how Horace Danby planned his robbery of Shotover Grange. Or Horace was the thief who planned his work carefully. Describe what he did before attempting to rob the house at Shotover Grange.
items.answer: A magazine article had described the house Shotover Grange, giving a plan of all the rooms and a picture of the room where the safe was located. The writer had even mentioned that a painting hid the safe. He had studied the house, looking at its rooms, its electric wiring, its paths and gardens for two weeks. He knew that the family lived in London and the two servants who remained in the house had gone to watch movie that afternoon. So he was sure that it was going to be a successful robbery.

items.stem: Describe how the lady in red was a more professional thief than Horace Danby. Or How did the lady in red prove to be smarter and cleverer than Horace Danby?
items.answer: Horace Danby missed to get enough information about all the members of the house. He seems to be too occupied with collecting information about house map, wiring and location of valuable things. Although he was smart enough to know the dog’s actual name but overlooked getting identity of each and every member of the house. Once he was in problem then probably his clever mind gave way to carelessness leading him to open the safe without wearing gloves. On the other hand, the young lady’s confident walk, her act of touching up her make-up and the ease with which she picked cigarette from the right place were enough to make Horace believe that she was lady of the house. Horace was too frightened to think properly so he didn’t suspect anything.

items.stem: Why did Horace choose that house in Shotover Grange for committing a theft ?
items.answer: Horace knew that there were about fifteen thousand pounds worth of jewels in the safe of that house in Shotover Grange. That is why, he decided to commit a theft in that house. He expected to get at least five thousand pounds by selling the jewels one by one, which would make him happy for another year. Horace wanted this money to buy three very interesting books, which were coming for sale the next winter. Moreover, a magazine article had described that house in detail, giving a plan of all the rooms along with the pictures. The magazine had even mentioned that the painting in the room hid the safe. On top of that, the two servants had gone to the movies and the family was in London. Because of all of these circumstances, Horace Danby had chosen that house as the place for committing a theft.

items.stem: Horace Danby represents such people who adopt the wrong ways to fulfil their wishes. What values would you like such people to imbibe to reform themselves?
items.answer: Horace Danby was a successful businessman. He was about fifty years old and a respectable citizen but had a habit that led him to do robberies. Danby loved rare, expensive books and to get them he used to rob a safe every year. Every year he planned carefully just to get what he wanted. Danby adopted wrong ways to fulfil his wishes and hence, later got trapped in a plot by a thief like him. People should imbibe good values. They should learn that hard work is the only key to success. One should work hard to fulfil one’s desires. I think such people should imbibe the values of honesty, responsibility, hard work, dedication and self-confidence in order to reform themselves. One should either curb one’s wishes or try to fulfil them by working hard. There is no shortcut to hard work.

items.stem: “Horace had some hope because she seemed to be amused at meeting him.” Why did Horace feel so? Did he consider the young lady compassionate towards him? Did he find her free from biases? Discuss the values Horace should have imbibe understanding of the person.
items.answer: Horace was a fifty-year-old man who used to rob only to buy rare and expensive. This time he decided to rob Shot over Grange. But as soon as he entered the room, a young lady appeared. She posed to be the lady of the house. She was very confident in her way of mannerism. Then she tried to be polite and nice to him. On hearing her, Horace felt that he had a hope of escaping. He found her a bit compassionate towards him. He was amused at Horace. She acted in quite a subtle manner and showed her sympathy and admiration towards a simple and honest man. He could not judge her ace. She made Horace promise that he would never commit the crime again. Horace should have been clever, shrewd and witty like the lady.

He decided to steal money from the clergyman’s house. He made himself invisible and entered his study. The clergyman and his wife woke-up, when they heard noise in their study. He hit the shopkeeper and stole his money. At the inn he entered the clergyman’s study and stole money from his desk. Thus he proved to be an eccentric scientist who used his scientific knowledge for wrong doings and posed a threat to the society. He misused his scientific discovery. If even I become invisible I would try to use this for spreading message of peace over humanity. If I realise that I can scatter wealth to help the poor even if it is at the cost of rich people, I would feel delighted. At times invisibility can be a great help to spy over the enemies and to catch the culprits.

items.stem: Are there forces around us that are invisible, for example, magnetism? Are there aspects of matter that are “invisible” or not visible to the naked eye ? What would the world be like if you could see such forces or such aspects of matter ?
items.answer: There are many forces around us that are invisible. For example, magnetism or the gravitational force is the force which we can feel but cannot see. It is the existence of such a force which has held the planets in their respective position and make the things fall to the earth. Had these forces not existed we would have been floating in the atmosphere. Some heavenly bodies can be seen with the help of the naked eye. While there are some stars which cannot be seen with the help of naked eyes. Such stars are so far off that visibility is not possible. If we could see such forces then the world would be surrounded by various rays which will be crossing each other like a maze. The confusion will be so great that one will not be able to understand which path to follow or which is restricted.

items.stem: A character arc is the transformation or development of a character throughout a story and refers to the changes a character undergoes as a result of his/her experiences, challenges and interactions with other characters. In light of the above information, trace the character arc of Griffin in H.G. Wells’ Footprints without Feet’.
items.answer: Griffin in H.G. Wells’ ‘Footprints without Feet’ undergoes a significant character arc throughout the story. Initially, he is portrayed as a brilliant yet eccentric scientist obsessed with achieving invisibility. However, as the narrative progresses, his obsession leads him down a path of moral degradation. Griffin’s character arc is marked by his descent into madness and amorality as he abuses his newfound power of invisibility for personal gain and revenge. By the end of the story, Griffin’s transformation is complete, culminating in his tragic demise as a cautionary tale about the dangers of unchecked ambition and hubris.

items.stem: Did Griffin from ‘Footprints without Feet’ follow the saying ‘With great power comes great responsibility’? Justify your answer in 120 words.
items.answer: No, Griffin did not follow the saying ‘with great power comes great responsibility’. Since Griffin did not think of anyone else except himself, this saying is not what he followed. After he managed to make himself invisible, he did not use his powers of invisibility for good. Instead, one of the first things he did was set fire to his landlord’s house in an act of revenge. He did not think of helping anyone with his newfound powers; instead, he harmed other people for his own gain. He stole clothes and food for himself without feeling any remorse. When his money ran low once more, he again resorted to stealing and robbed a clergyman. Finally, when the police were about to catch him, instead of going quietly and accepting his arrest, he fought back and escaped. At no time did Griffin take any responsibility for his actions.

items.stem: How can one become a scientist, an economist, a historian Does it simply involve reading many books on the subject? Does it involve observing; thinking and doing experiments?
items.answer: One can perform a job to the best of his capabilities if one is really interested in it. Once we choose a goal or an aim, we should strive hard to achieve it. I think reading books is just one aspect of learning. This is an exercise in information gathering. It is how your brain processes the information that affects the degree of learning. The first and the foremost criterion to become a genius in one’s chosen field is to have great curiosity and unending hunger to discover more. Next criterion is a good sense of observation which helps you correlate your findings with what you see or experience in the real world. Experiments are must to test your findings against possible variables and in real life situations. And last, but not the least criterion is an urge to work really hard on your area of interest. Hard work is actually the key to success. One should have perseverance and strong will- power to achieve what one aspires to.

They also appear to have a good memory. They try to find through a clever dance language. The dance indicates the direction and distance of the food source. Thus they have a well developed direction finding mechanism and a way of reckoning distance. (iii) Rain is formed as a result of condensation of vapour when air is cooled below the dew point. The raindrops start out as tiny ice crystals and on the way they collect moisture. The crystals change into water droplets and fall on the ground as drops.

items.stem: “When he saw those photos.” Which photos did he see and what discovery did this lead to ?
items.answer: He saw photos of the chemical structure of a hormone in the X-ray. This photo enabled him to answer one of the biology puzzles. His doubt on DNA was solved. items.stem: Albert Einstein said, ‘The important thing is to never stop questioning.’ Richard was a genius who proved this quote true. Justify.

items.stem: Richard Ebright displayed a well-rounded personality. Do you agree ? Elucidate in the context of the given text.

items.stem: What was the impact of the book ‘The Travels of Monarch X’ on Richard Ebright ?
items.answer: Richard Ebright had started collecting butterflies when he was in kindergarten. So, to maintain his interest in this field in his later years, his mother had got him a children’s book called ‘The Travels of Monarch X.’ This book had told how monarch butterflies migrate to Central America. The impact of this book was so strong on Ebright’s mind that it opened the world of science for him. At the end of this book, readers had been invited to help study butterfly migrations. They had been asked to tag butterflies for research by Dr. Frederick A. Urquhart of the university of Toronto, Canada. Ebright’s mother wrote to Dr. Urquhart, and soon Ebright was also taking part in the study by attaching light adhesive tags to the wings of the monarchs. According to the research, anyone who found a tagged butterfly was asked to send the tag to Dr. Urquhart. Ultimately, it was Richard’s fascination for butterflies that opened the world of science to him. It also indirectly led to his theory on how cells work.

items.stem: Dr Urquhart contributed significantly to Ebright’s growth as a scientist. Explain.

The discovery of this new hormone further led to an important theory. The theory was about how cells read their DNA. In this way Dr. Urquhart proved to be his true mentor.

items.answer: Life underwent a lot of change when because of the necklace Loisel fell in a debt trap which forced her to live like an ordinary lower middle class housewife. items.stem: What is the twist at the end of the story ‘The Necklace’?
items.answer: The twist at the end of the story “The Necklace” is the fact that Mathilde borrowed the necklace to appear more beautiful but ended up losing her beauty completely. She borrows Madame Forestier’s necklace made with fake diamonds to give the appearance of being rich but lost both her money and looks.

items.stem: How does the writer’s use of the literary device a twist in the tale, towards the story’s end, impact the narrative of ‘The Necklace’?
items.answer: It significantly impacts the narrative. The revelation that the lost necklace was a mere imitation rather than a valuable piece turns the story on its head. This twist adds irony, and highlights the story’s theme of materialism. The impact leaves a lasting impression on our understanding of the characters’ choices and the consequences of relentless desire. It transforms the narrative into a cautionary tale, and makes us reflect on the true worth of one’s aspirations.

items.stem: How does the story, ‘The Necklace’ teach a moral lesson on the importance of contentment?
items.answer: The story teaches a powerful moral lesson on the importance of finding contentment in what one already has. Matilda’s desire for social status and material possessions led to her own downfall and a decade of hardship. Had Matilda simply been grateful and content with all that she had, she could have avoided a lot of pain.

items.stem: What changes came in the lifestyle of Matilda after she had lost the necklace?
items.answer: After the loss of the necklace, Matilda had to sacrifice all her comforts and even all her needs to get money to buy a new necklace and give it to her friend. items.answer: Matilda’s husband had saved a substantial amount of money to buy a gun for himself, so that he could join the hunting parties the next summer. But, he gave the entire money to Matilda to buy a pretty dress for herself to go to the ball.

items.stem: How and when did, Matilda find the borrowed necklace missing?
items.answer: Matilda went home from the ball at about four o’clock in the morning. After reaching home, she removed the wraps from her shoulder before the glass so that she could have a final view of her glory. It was at that time that she found her necklace missing.

items.stem: How did Matilda gain time from Mme Forestier for returning her necklace?
items.answer: When the lost necklace was not found, Matilda wrote to her friend Mme Forestier that she had broken the clasp of the necklace, and it had been sent for repairs. She did so to gain time for arranging money to buy a similar necklace.

items.stem: What did Matilda’s husband bring home one evening? Why was he so elated?
items.answer: One evening, Matilda’s husband brought an invitation card inviting them to the residence of the Minister of Public Instruction. He was quite elated to receive the invitation because it was a rare honour, and on top of that, he thought that his wife would feel delighted to attend the ball.

items.stem: What happened at the ball ? Was her dream fulfilled?
items.answer: At the ball, Matilda was drunk with pleasure and filled with joy. She danced joyfully and excitedly. Fascinated with her charm and beauty, all the men wanted to be introduced to her. The officials of the ministry even desired to dance with her. She danced with passion and forgot everything in the victory of her glory.

items.stem: What was the financial position of Matilda’s husband?
items.answer: Matilda’s husband was a petty clerk in the office of the Board of Education. He was both poor and economical. He could not afford even to purchase a party dress or some jewels for his wife. She had to attend the dance party after borrowing a necklace from Mrs. Forestier. He had to do menial jobs to earn paltry sums.

items.stem: What were the changes that take place in Matilda’s life after the ball?
items.answer: After the ball Matilda lost Mrs. Forestier’s necklace. She and her husband bought a chaplet of diamonds by borrowing eighteen thousand francs. Both the husband and wife led a life of misery. Matilda send away the maid. She lived in a rented room and did all the household work. She lived a wretched life for ten years.

items.stem: A character arc is the transformation or development of a character throughout a story and refers to the changes a character undergoes as a result of their experiences, challenges, and interactions with other characters. In the light of the above information, trace the character arc of Matilda in Guy De Maupassants ‘The Necklace’, in about 120 words.
items.answer: Mathilde Loisel is the protagonist of Guy de Maupassant’s The Necklace, a short story that depicts her character arc from a dissatisfied and vain woman to a humble and hardworking one. Mathilde’s character arc is driven by the events and consequences of losing a borrowed diamond necklace, which she wears to a high-society party to impress others and escape her middle-class life. At the beginning of the story, Mathilde is unhappy with her modest lifestyle and marriage. She believes that she deserves more wealth, luxury, and admiration, and she envies her rich friend Madame Forestier. She is obsessed with appearance and status, and she neglects the simple pleasures and comforts that her husband provides. She is also ungrateful and selfish, as she does not appreciate her husband’s efforts to please her and make her happy.

items.stem: Imagine that M. Loisel, from The Necklace by Guy de Maupassant, writes a diary entry, exploring the theme of class and social status, and the nature of social mobility, in the context of his own experience. Write this diary entry, as M. Loisel, in about 120 words.
items.answer: November 19XX, Wednesday 9:00 pm 9 p.m. Dear Diary Today, I recall my experience of class and social status and the predicaments it brought to me and my wife Matilda. Both me and my wife were happy until one night we fell into this ugly trap of upward social mobility which leads to the destruction of houses. This whole circle of social mobility, from end to top, is quite vicious. The rich gets richer while the poor gets poorer. The middle class gets entirely stuck in between and tries to make ends meet with his little bucks but pretends to be classy. Matilda was too a victim of this fake pretence and this gave us a very tough time for several years when she lost the borrowed necklace. Had she not tried to pretend the upper class that night, we would have been living a different life. People should never lose their happiness for such unattainable dreams. M. Loisel

items.stem: Mme Forestier writes a diary entry after having met Matilda, knowing the truth and seeing the transformation in her friend. Write a short diary entry as Mme Forestier about your encounter and how you felt. You may begin like this: 20th July, Monday 9:00 pm I couldn’t recognise Matilda at all. I wish she had told me the truth about the necklace.
items.answer: 20th July, Monday 9:00 pm Dear diary, I couldn’t recognise Matilda at all. I wish she had told me the truth about the necklace. She had to undergo a troubled life to repay the price of the necklace which was actually 400 francs only. She is no more a pretty woman now. I am surprised that despite being sharing good relations with each other she did not share the news about the accidental loss of the piece of jewellery. I remember that she always criticised her status. But, the hard time has made her realise that one should value their possessions. That’s all for now. Bye

items.stem: Your teacher conducted Turn Tables in class, and asked you to put forth your views on ‘Frugality in Life is the Ideal Way to Live’. Write the debate script with points to supplement your stand, both for and against the motion and conclude with your own views.
items.answer: Frugality in Life is the Ideal Way to Live I have always heard from my parents that a penny saved is a penny earned. For many years, I did not like their idealism of spend thriftiness. If we have the resources we should use them fully because life is so uncertain. Moreover, a phase in life gone never comes back. So, one should have a big heart to enjoy life to the fullest. But, life taught me a lesson when Covid 19 hit the world and specifically my family badly. During that time the money that my parents saved miserly helped us to sustain. Now, I had understood that we should not waste our resources unnecessarily. If we adopt minimalism, we can help the poor and needy and hence the nation. Spending money on useless things does not serve any purpose. Money keeps changing hands. Life is so uncertain, today’s meagre savings can become a great reliever in times of need. So, I believe that ‘Frugality in Life is the ideal way to live’.

items.stem: Ostentation and vanity often land people in trouble. Matilda is an apt example of this. Justify. Or Matilda wanted to live a life above her status. How did this desire of hers lead to her sufferings?
items.answer: Matilda always wanted a life above her status. This desire of hers had led her to sufferings as for the party she had borrowed her friend’s diamond necklace. After the party when she lost it she decided to bend the truth. She lied that the necklaces’ clasp was broken and it was away for mending. She instead bought a very similar looking diamond necklace. Due to that she and her husband were under the debt of many people. They had to shift into a new and a smaller apartment, She had to leave the maid and do everything by herself, She had to bargain for every penny, Her voice had become cracked and she seemed old and weary. When she told her friend about the four painful years she was shocked and told Matilda that her necklace was an imitation one and it did not cost over five hundred francs.

items.stem: Give the character-sketch of Matilda.
items.answer: Matilda was a pretty and young lady. She was born in the family of clerks and was married to a clerk. Having been born in a poor family she had no dowry, no hopes, no means of becoming known, loved or married by some rich man of dignity. She always suffered from poverty both at the homes of her husband and parents. She was a short-tempered but tactful lady. She convinced her poor husband to buy her a party dress simply by rejecting the invitation to the ball. She was of showy nature and loved only delicacies and luxuries. She borrowed a necklace only to be noticed by the spectators. She repented when the necklace was lost. She suffered poverty for ten years after replacing the false necklace with a genuine necklace. She ever remained in distress. She was not a considerate and contented character.

items.stem: Give the character-sketch of Mr. Loisel.
items.answer: Mr. Loisel was a petty clerk in the office of the Board of Education. He had no other source of income. Therefore, he lived from hand to mouth. He was very economical. He ate humble food in cheap dishes. He lived in a humble apartment. He was meek and gentle. He was considerate to the wishes of his short-tempered, pretty and sophisticated wife. Loisel forgoes buying a gun to purchase a pretty dress for his wife. To keep her in good cheer, he urged her to borrow a necklace from her friend. He tried his level best to search the lost necklace. He was adventurous. He did not hesitate in spending his entire inherited money and even borrowing from money-lenders to replace the lost necklace. He was of flexible nature but a man of good character. He was a loving husband and had poor tastes.

items.stem: Why did Jeanne not recognise her friend? Or Why could Mme Forestier not recognize her friend Matilda at the end of the story?
items.answer: Matilda had to undergo a lot of hardships and miseries to repay the debt. All this had happened because she had lost the necklace she had borrowed from her rich friend Mme Forestier or Jeanne. Because of this debt, they had to move to a cheaper room and even remain without a servant. Matilda had to do all the household work and shopping by herself. She had to fetch water, wash the floor, utensils and dirty clothes by herself. It took them ten years to finally repay the debt. But after those difficult ten years, Matilda now looked like an ordinary woman, wearing simple clothes. She even looked older than her age. That is why, Jeanne was not able to recognise Matilda.

items.stem: Why did Bholi at first agree to an unequal match? Why did she later reject the marriage? What does this tell us about her?
items.answer: It is the tradition in India that girls seldom oppose their parents’ choice for a groom. The upbringing of daughters brings a kind of mental conditioning which doesn’t give them enough courage to rebel against their parents’ wishes. Bholi more or less followed the tradition of being an ideal Indian girl. Later on when the prospective groom depicted his greed for money it repulsed Bholi and made her reject the marriage. This incident highlights the fact that education does produce some positive effects in terms of sense of empowerment. Unlike her sisters, Bholi is educated and has a mind of her own. She is as independent as any modern girl of a big city.

items.answer: The word Bholi means a simpleton. Throughout the story she had been a simpleton hardly expressing her opinion. The word Sulekha means the person with beautiful sense of letters. In this story this word has a larger meaning of being a literate, intelligent and mature individual. After her education Bholi has really changed to Sulekha and her assertion during marriage is her announcement to the world that she is no more a Bholi but Sulekha. She had been a suppressed child since her childhood. She was an innocent girl who didn’t have her own say. But her teacher helped her overcome social barriers by encouraging and motivating her. She then becomes more assertive and feels that there is a world beyond.

items.stem: Should girls be aware of their rights and asserts them? Should girls and boys have the same rights, duties and privileges? What are some of the ways in which society treats them differently? When we speak of ‘human rights’, do we differentiate between girls rights and boys rights?
items.answer: Yes, according to me girls should be aware of their rights as well as they should assert them. Boys and girls have equal rights and privileges. Even the law has granted them equal rights in property, job, etc. At present, women are excelling in every profession. The traditional trend to restrict women folk of the house to only domestic chores is still continuing, especially in rural areas. In rural areas, where the education and awareness are less, the boys are favoured than girls to the extent that they are given more nutritious diet and higher education than girls. People still believe that a person will be able to attain salvation only if his last rites are performed by his son. And the father’s name is carried forward only through a son. These false myths are chiefly responsible for girl infanticide. Innumerable girl foetus are destroyed through illegal sex detection. Hence when we speak about human rights, we do not differentiate between the rights of girls and boys. But the real picture is far different and grim than this.
